topics.title: Functions and Use of Digital Devices, and Notation

items.definition: General-purpose computers for one person: desktops and laptops.
items.examples: A designer's desktop; a student's laptop.
items.examTip: Desktop: more power for the price, upgradeable. Laptop: portable, battery, less upgradeable.
keyFacts: Key parts: CPU, RAM, storage, GPU
Run a full OS (Windows, macOS, Linux)
Used for office work, gaming, creative work

items.definition: One device that combines printing, scanning, copying and sometimes fax.
items.examples: An office printer/scanner/copier.
items.examTip: Saves space and money, but if it breaks, every function is lost.
keyFacts: Often networked: scan straight to email

items.definition: Portable battery-powered devices with a touchscreen and mobile OS, e.g. phones and tablets.
items.examples: iPhone; iPad; Apple Watch.
items.examTip: Always connected, but smaller screens, limited battery and easily lost.

items.definition: Powerful computers that provide files, apps or web pages to other computers on a network.
items.examples: A file server for shared documents; a web server hosting a website.
items.examTip: Know the three: file (stores files), application (runs software), web (serves pages).
keyFacts: Application server: runs apps for clients
Web server: delivers pages over HTTP/HTTPS

comparisonTable.title: Server Types Compared
rows: Stores and manages access to shared files/folders
Company shared drive (H: drive in Windows domain)
Hosts and runs software applications for network clients
Internal clients running client-side of the application
ERP system, database server, email server (Exchange)
Hosts website files, handles HTTP/HTTPS requests from browsers
Apache/Nginx hosting company website; IIS hosting intranet

items.definition: Devices mainly for leisure, e.g. games consoles, smart TVs and streaming sticks.
items.examples: PlayStation 5; a smart TV; Fire TV Stick.
items.examTip: Now internet-connected: link to streaming and online entertainment.

items.definition: Devices that capture photos or video digitally.
items.examples: DSLR; GoPro; CCTV; phone camera.
items.examTip: High-resolution photos and video need lots of storage and bandwidth.
keyFacts: More megapixels = better quality, bigger files

items.definition: Devices or apps that use GPS satellites to find your location and plan routes.
items.examples: A sat nav; Google Maps; tracking delivery vans.
items.examTip: GPS gives position; live traffic needs an internet connection.

items.definition: Hardware for sending and receiving information, e.g. phones, routers and modems.
items.examples: Mobile phones; VoIP phones; routers.
items.examTip: The hardware layer of networks: link to Section B.
keyFacts: Modem: converts signals for phone or cable lines
Router: connects the LAN to the internet
VoIP phones: calls over the internet

items.term: Embedded Systems (Sensors and Internet of Things)
items.definition: A computer built into a device to do one job; IoT devices are embedded systems connected to the internet.
items.examples: A washing machine controller; a smart thermostat; a smart meter.
items.examTip: Embedded = one fixed job. IoT = embedded + internet. IoT security is often weak.
keyFacts: Single purpose, little or no interface
IoT devices send data to the cloud
Weak default passwords and rare updates

subtopics.title: Function and Use of Digital Devices by Context

items.definition: Using devices for everyday tasks: communication, entertainment, shopping and banking.
items.examTip: Consider privacy when discussing personal use.
keyFacts: Phones for messaging, maps and media
Smart speakers and thermostats at home

items.term: Education and Training Use of Digital Devices
items.definition: Using devices to support teaching, learning and assessment.
items.examTip: Link to online education and the digital divide.

items.definition: Using devices to communicate and interact with others online.
items.examTip: Give both sides: connection and support vs cyberbullying and addiction.

items.definition: Using devices to support buying, selling and managing stock.
items.examTip: Link to online retail and stock control.

items.definition: Using computer-controlled machines, robots and sensors to automate manufacturing.
items.examTip: Key themes: CNC machines, robots, sensors for quality control.
keyFacts: Sensors monitor machines in real time

items.definition: Using devices for diagnosis, treatment, monitoring and admin in healthcare.
items.examTip: Must be highly reliable; patient data is very sensitive.

items.definition: Using devices for design, music, video, animation and photography.
items.examTip: Creative work needs powerful hardware and lots of fast storage.

items.definition: Machines and AI doing repetitive or complex tasks with little human input.
items.examples: Warehouse robots; car assembly lines; chatbots.
items.examTip: Efficiency vs job losses and retraining needs.

subtopics.title: Forms of Notation for IT System Design

items.definition: Diagrams showing a system's components and how they connect.
items.examples: A network diagram of PCs, switch, router, server and internet.
items.examTip: Exam diagrams (6 marks): include every device from the scenario and label each connection type.

items.definition: Diagrams showing the steps of a process using standard symbols.
items.examples: A login process checking a password.
items.examTip: Learn the symbols: oval start/end, rectangle process, diamond decision, parallelogram input/output.

comparisonTable.title: System Diagram vs Flowchart
rows: Components of an IT system and their connections
Steps in a process or algorithm and their sequence
Logic, decisions, data flow through a process
Designing or documenting processes, algorithms, programs
Draw a network/system showing how components connect
Complete or draw a process showing steps and decisions

subtopics.title: Features and Uses of Peripheral Devices

items.definition: Hardware for getting data into a computer.
items.examples: Keyboard; mouse; microphone; barcode scanner; touchscreen.
items.examTip: Input = data going IN. Manual (keyboard) or automatic (sensor, scanner).
keyFacts: Optical: scanner, barcode and QR readers, camera

items.definition: Hardware that presents results from a computer to people.
items.examples: Monitor; printer; speakers; projector; braille display.
items.examTip: Output = data coming OUT. Printers make hard copy; screens make soft copy.

items.definition: Hardware that keeps data so it can be used again later.
items.examples: Laptop SSD; external backup drive; USB stick.
items.examTip: Compare HDD and SSD on speed, cost and reliability.
keyFacts: HDD: spinning disk, cheap per GB
SSD: flash, faster, no moving parts
USB sticks and external drives for transfer
NAS: shared storage on a network

items.definition: Keyboards adapted for users with physical, visual or learning difficulties.
items.examples: Large-key keyboards; one-handed keyboards.
items.examTip: For users who cannot use a standard keyboard.
keyFacts: Large keys for low vision or motor difficulties

items.definition: Software that reads screen content aloud for blind or partially sighted users.
items.examples: JAWS; NVDA; VoiceOver.
items.examTip: Only works well if sites and apps are built accessibly.
keyFacts: Reads text, menus and buttons aloud
Used with the keyboard, not a mouse

items.definition: A device that raises pins to form braille, so blind users can read the screen by touch.
items.examples: A refreshable braille display connected by USB.
items.examTip: Tactile output that updates as the screen changes.

items.definition: Software that enlarges part or all of the screen for users with low vision.
items.examples: Windows Magnifier; zoom on macOS.
items.examTip: Makes things bigger, rather than reading them aloud.

items.definition: A stick or pointer worn on the head so users can press keys without using their hands.
items.examples: A head stick used by someone with paralysis.
items.examTip: For users with little or no arm or hand movement.
keyFacts: Head-tracking cameras are the electronic version

items.definition: A single button that lets users with very limited movement control a computer.
items.examples: A large button switch; a cheek switch.
items.examTip: The computer cycles through options; the user presses to select.
keyFacts: Scanning highlights each option in turn
Any reliable movement can work the switch

items.definition: A pedal pressed by foot to trigger an action, keeping hands free.
items.examples: A pedal to pause audio while typing.
items.examTip: Assistive for users who can't use their hands, and a productivity tool.
keyFacts: Helps users with arm or hand impairments

items.definition: A switch controlled by sucking or blowing into a tube.
items.examples: Controlling a wheelchair and computer by breath.
items.examTip: For users who can only reliably control their breathing.
keyFacts: Sip and puff act as different inputs

items.definition: A camera that tracks where the user looks so they can control the cursor with their eyes.
items.examples: Tobii eye trackers for people with motor neurone disease.
items.examTip: Looking at a target for a moment (dwell) acts as a click.

items.definition: Software that reads written text aloud as speech.
items.examples: Read Aloud in Word; communication apps for non-verbal users.
items.examTip: Helps people who can't read easily, and lets non-verbal users speak.
keyFacts: Helps with dyslexia and visual impairment
Built into all major operating systems

subtopics.title: Characteristics and Implications of Storage Media

items.definition: How much data a storage medium can hold, measured in GB or TB.
items.examTip: Match capacity to the use: video editing needs TBs; documents need GBs.
keyFacts: USB sticks: tens to hundreds of GB

items.definition: The price of storage, especially the cost per gigabyte.
items.examTip: HDD is cheapest per GB; SSD costs more but is falling; cloud is an ongoing fee.
keyFacts: SSD: worth it for the OS drive

comparisonTable.title: Storage Media Compared: HDD vs SSD vs USB vs Optical
rows: Fragile — moving parts, vulnerable to drops

items.definition: How fast data is read from and written to storage.
items.examTip: Moving from HDD to SSD is the biggest speed upgrade for most computers.

items.definition: Whether the storage works with the device's connections, OS and hardware.
items.examTip: Check the connector, the file system and OS support.
keyFacts: Connectors: USB-A vs USB-C, SATA vs NVMe
Older devices may not support new drives

items.definition: Data entered and handled by people rather than computers.
items.examples: Writing appointments in a paper diary; counting stock by hand.
items.examTip: Slower and more error-prone, but flexible where judgement is needed.

items.definition: Data collected and processed by computers with little or no human input.
items.examples: EPOS updating stock at each sale; overnight bank processing.
items.examTip: Faster and more consistent. But a system error affects every record.
keyFacts: Batch: processed together at set times

comparisonTable.title: Manual vs Automatic Data Processing
rows: Computer systems with minimal human input
Slow — limited by human working speed
Consistent — but systematic errors if algorithm is wrong
High initial setup; lower ongoing cost
Lower — may struggle with exceptions to normal rules
Can scale to process millions of transactions
Receptionist writing appointments in paper diary
EPOS system auto-updating stock when items are scanned

topics.title: Computer Software in an IT System

items.definition: An OS that processes groups of jobs automatically, without user interaction.
items.examples: Overnight bank payments; monthly payroll.
items.examTip: No interaction, runs in groups, often overnight. Results are not instant.

items.definition: An OS that makes many separate computers work together as one system.
items.examples: Google spreading searches across thousands of servers.
items.examTip: Many computers acting as one: fault tolerant and scalable.
keyFacts: One machine failing doesn't stop the system

items.definition: An OS that runs several programs at once by switching the CPU between them quickly.
items.examples: Browsing while music plays and a file downloads.
items.examTip: The CPU switches so fast it seems simultaneous.
keyFacts: Needs enough RAM for all open programs

items.definition: An OS on a server that manages shared files, printers and user accounts for a network.
items.examples: Windows Server.
items.examTip: Runs on servers; clients connect for files, printers and logins.

items.definition: An OS that must respond to inputs within a guaranteed, very short time.
items.examples: ABS brakes; aircraft controls; a pacemaker.
items.examTip: About being predictable, not just fast. Used where delay is dangerous.
keyFacts: Used in medical, transport and industrial systems

items.definition: An OS designed for phones, tablets and wearables.
items.examples: iOS; Android.
items.examTip: Built for touch, battery life and apps from app stores.

items.definition: A stripped-down OS that does one job only.
items.examples: An ATM; a self-service kiosk.
items.examTip: Reliable and secure, but can't be used for anything else.

items.definition: An OS that lets several users use the same system at once, each with their own account.
items.examples: A Linux server with many remote users.
items.examTip: Must keep each user's files and sessions separate.
keyFacts: Each user has a private session

comparisonTable.title: Operating System Types Compared
rows: Processes jobs in groups without user interaction
Multiple programs appear to run simultaneously
Office server managing files and users
Multiple simultaneous users with isolated sessions

subtopics.title: Role of the Operating System in Managing

items.definition: The OS handles network protocols, connections, sending and receiving data, and bandwidth.
items.examTip: Four parts: protocols, connections, transmission, resource monitoring.
keyFacts: Splits data into packets and reassembles them
Assigns IP settings, e.g. via DHCP

items.definition: The OS protects the system through access control, malware protection, encryption and a firewall.
items.examTip: Know the four areas and what each does.

items.definition: The OS gives RAM to programs, keeps them apart, and uses virtual memory when RAM runs out.
items.examTip: Name the parts: allocation, protection, virtual memory, swapping and paging.
keyFacts: Allocates RAM when a program starts and frees it when it ends
Programs can't touch each other's memory
Virtual memory: disk used as extra RAM (slower)
Paging swaps small blocks between RAM and disk

items.definition: The OS shares CPU time between running programs by scheduling and switching between them.
items.examTip: Name the parts: scheduling, CPU time management, context switching.
keyFacts: Scheduling decides which process runs next
Round robin: equal time slices in turn
Context switching saves and restores each process

items.definition: Software that lets the OS talk to a hardware device.
items.examTip: Without the right driver, the OS can't use the device.
keyFacts: Translates OS commands for the device
Outdated drivers cause crashes and security holes
items.examples: A printer driver; a graphics card driver.

items.definition: The OS checks who users are, stores their settings, and lets admins manage accounts.
items.examTip: Name the parts: authentication, profiles, account management tools.
keyFacts: Log in with password, PIN, biometric or MFA
Each user has their own profile and files

subtopics.title: Types, Uses and Features of Software

items.definition: Software that maintains and looks after the computer system.
items.examples: Antivirus; backup; disk defragmenter; file compression.
items.examTip: Utility software maintains the system. It is not application software.

items.definition: Software people use to do tasks and create things.
items.examples: Word; Excel; Photoshop; a web browser.
items.examTip: Application software is for doing work, not maintaining the system.
keyFacts: Can be general or specialist, e.g. CAD

subtopics.title: Factors Impacting Choice of OS and Application Software

items.definition: The cost of buying, licensing and running software.
items.examTip: Open source is often free; proprietary has licence fees but vendor support.

items.definition: How well software protects data, including how often it gets security updates.
items.examTip: Especially important when choosing an OS.
keyFacts: Windows is targeted most because it's most used
Open-source code can be checked by anyone

items.definition: Whether software works with the hardware and other software already in use.
items.examTip: Incompatible software is useless however good it is.
keyFacts: Drivers exist for existing printers and devices

items.definition: Whether the software has the functions the organisation needs.
items.examTip: Features must match the job; extras add cost and complexity.
keyFacts: Specialist tools may only be proprietary

items.definition: Whether the software fits the organisation's tasks and its users' skills.
items.examTip: Start here in scenarios: what must it do, and who will use it?

items.definition: How well the software runs on the available hardware.
items.examTip: Heavy software on weak hardware = slow and unproductive.

items.definition: A text interface where the user types commands.
items.examples: Command Prompt; Linux Terminal.
items.examTip: Fast and powerful for experts, but commands must be memorised.

items.definition: An interface where users choose from a list of options.
items.examples: ATM screens; "press 1 for sales" phone menus.
items.examTip: Simple and guided, but limited to the options shown.
keyFacts: Can't do anything not on the menu

items.definition: A visual interface with windows, icons, menus and a pointer (WIMP).
items.examples: The Windows desktop; macOS.
items.examTip: Easiest for non-technical users, but uses more resources than a CLI.
keyFacts: Slower than CLI for repetitive tasks

items.definition: A GUI controlled by touch gestures instead of a mouse.
items.examples: Smartphones; self-checkouts.
items.examTip: Needs bigger buttons; ideal for phones and kiosks.
keyFacts: Used on phones, tablets and kiosks

subtopics.title: Principles and Implications of Open Source and Proprietary Software

items.term: Open Source vs Proprietary Operating Systems
items.definition: Open-source OS code is free to view and change (Linux); proprietary code is closed (Windows, macOS).
items.examples: Linux vs Windows; Android vs iOS.
items.examTip: Give advantages AND disadvantages of both.
keyFacts: Open source: less polished, patchy driver support
Proprietary: licence costs, locked to one vendor

comparisonTable.title: Open Source vs Proprietary Software
rows: Publicly available — can be viewed, modified, redistributed
Closed — only vendor can access and modify
Community forums, documentation, optional paid support
Vendor provides dedicated support (often included or paid)
Many eyes on the code — bugs found quickly; also visible to attackers
Vendor controls patches; smaller attack surface visibility; faster coordinated response
Highly customisable — modify code for specific needs
Limited customisation — only features vendor provides
May have driver/compatibility issues with some hardware or proprietary formats
Designed to work with mainstream hardware; vendor-controlled ecosystem
Low — can switch, fork, or modify freely

items.term: Open Source vs Proprietary Application Software
items.definition: The same open-source vs proprietary choice, applied to applications.
items.examples: LibreOffice vs Microsoft 365; GIMP vs Photoshop.
items.examTip: Also consider file compatibility: proprietary formats may not open correctly.
keyFacts: Free alternatives may lack advanced features
Some industries require specific proprietary tools
Saving licence fees can cost more in support

subtopics.title: Features of Common File Types and Formats

items.definition: Image formats differ in compression, quality and features.
items.examples: JPEG photos; PNG logos; SVG icons.
items.examTip: JPEG lossy (photos); PNG lossless (transparency); SVG scalable; RAW largest.

items.definition: Audio formats differ in compression, size and quality.
items.examples: MP3 streaming; WAV recording.
items.examTip: MP3/AAC for streaming; WAV/FLAC for production. Higher bit rate = better and bigger.

items.definition: A video file is a container (e.g. MP4) holding streams compressed by a codec.
items.examples: MP4 online; MOV from Apple devices.
items.examTip: H.265 is half the size of H.264 at the same quality.

items.definition: Installer and program formats specific to each operating system.
items.examples: EXE/MSI on Windows; DMG on macOS; APK on Android.
items.examTip: Only install from trusted sources and check digital signatures.
keyFacts: EXE runs programs; MSI installs them

subtopics.title: Factors Affecting the Choice of IT Systems

items.definition: What the people using the system need: their tasks, skills, mobility and accessibility needs.
items.examTip: Always start with user needs: who will use it and what for?

items.definition: The technical requirements the system must meet, e.g. performance, storage and ports.
Whether the system works with existing hardware, software, data and networks.
keyFacts: Works with existing devices and software
Existing data can be moved across

items.definition: The network and device connections the system supports.
keyFacts: Ports to match peripherals: USB, HDMI

items.definition: The total cost of buying, setting up, running and replacing the system.
items.examTip: Consider total cost of ownership, not just the purchase price.

items.definition: How well the system uses time, money and resources to do its job.
Practicalities of rollout: timescales, testing, moving data and downtime.
items.examTip: Cover all four: timescales, testing, migration, downtime.
keyFacts: Rollout can take weeks or months
Test with real users before go-live
Moving data risks loss or corruption
Phased rollout or running old and new side by side reduces risk

items.definition: How the system affects how much work staff can get done.
The security features of the system and how it fits existing security measures.
Systems that track stock in real time and reorder automatically when it runs low.
items.examples: Supermarket tills reducing stock counts at each sale.
items.examTip: Benefits: fewer stockouts, less overstock. Risk: if it fails, stock levels are unknown.
keyFacts: Barcodes/RFID update stock at the till

items.definition: Sensors or systems automatically recording time-stamped readings over time.
items.examples: A weather station; factory temperature sensors.
items.examTip: Automatic, continuous and time-stamped. Link to IoT sensors.

items.definition: Using IT to find patterns and trends in data to guide decisions.
items.examples: Choosing which products to promote from sales data; spotting fraud.
items.examTip: Turns raw data into decisions.
keyFacts: Decisions based on evidence, not guesswork

items.definition: IT for everyday admin: documents, spreadsheets, email and scheduling.
items.examples: Microsoft 365; Teams; Zoom.

items.definition: IT for design, media production and animation.
items.examples: Photoshop; AutoCAD; Blender.
keyFacts: Large files need fast, big storage

items.definition: IT for creating, targeting and measuring adverts.
items.examples: Google Ads; Facebook ad targeting.
keyFacts: Link to targeted marketing and ethics

items.definition: IT that designs, controls and checks manufacturing, from CAD to quality control.
items.examples: CAD designs sent to CNC machines.
keyFacts: CAM: turns designs into machine instructions

items.definition: IT for physical and cyber security, e.g. CCTV and access control.
items.examples: Networked CCTV; biometric locks on a server room.
keyFacts: Creates lots of data to store

items.definition: IT performing tasks with little or no human input.
items.examples: Automated payroll; chatbots; robot arms.

subtopics.title: Impact and Implications of IT Systems on Organisations

items.term: User Experience (Ease of Use, Performance, Availability, Accessibility)
items.definition: How easy, fast, available and accessible a system is for staff and customers.
items.examTip: Cover all four: ease of use, performance, availability, accessibility.
keyFacts: Easy to use: fewer errors, less training

items.definition: Whether the system meets the needs of both staff and customers.
keyFacts: Staff need the right features without extra work
Customers need reliable and easy systems

items.definition: The cost of the system to the organisation, now and over time.
How the rollout affects the organisation: timescales, testing, data migration and downtime.
items.examTip: Focus on the impact during and after rollout.
keyFacts: Data can be lost when moving

items.term: Replacement or Integration with Current Systems
items.definition: Whether the new system replaces the old one entirely or works alongside it.
items.examTip: Replace: clean break but risky and costly. Integrate: lower risk but more complex.
keyFacts: Full replacement: higher risk and cost

items.definition: How the system affects staff output during and after the change.
keyFacts: Automation frees staff for other work

items.definition: How the system changes the way staff work.
Training staff need to use the system, at launch and as it changes.
items.examTip: Training costs time and money, but too little leads to errors and poor adoption.

items.definition: Ongoing help for staff using the system.
keyFacts: FAQs and guides reduce helpdesk load

items.definition: The new security risks a system brings and how it must be protected.
keyFacts: Set permissions carefully from day one

items.term: How Emerging Technologies and AI Affect IT System Performance
items.definition: AI and new technologies such as 5G and edge computing make systems faster and more capable.
items.examples: AI chips in phones; 5G for real-time applications.
items.examTip: Performance gains, but they need new infrastructure and lots of computing power.
keyFacts: AI chips run AI tasks much faster
Edge computing processes data near its source, cutting delay
5G: very fast with very low latency
AI tunes systems by learning from use

items.term: Implications of Emerging Technologies and AI on Personal Use of IT Systems
items.definition: How AI changes everyday personal use, from voice assistants to AI-generated content.
items.examples: Siri and Alexa; Netflix recommendations; deepfakes.
items.examTip: Give both sides: convenience and accessibility vs privacy, misinformation and over-reliance.

items.term: Implications of Emerging Technologies and AI on Organisations
items.definition: How AI and emerging technology change the way organisations operate and employ people.
items.examples: AI fraud detection in banks; AI screening job applications.
items.examTip: Both sides for Level 3: efficiency and better decisions vs job losses, bias and security.
keyFacts: Bias in training data; attackers use AI too
